analysis.one_liner: Lets the president waive any federal law to fast-track energy projects like pipelines and refineries.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: with zero cosponsors, it sat in House subcommittees until the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let the president, or anyone the president picked, wave aside any federal legal requirement standing in the way of an energy project — oil and gas pipelines, refineries, power lines, or drilling and energy leases on federal lands. The waiver would apply to any law at all, including the rules that let citizens file administrative protests against agency decisions. The only court challenge allowed would be a claim that the president violated the Constitution, filed within 60 days, with no appeals below the Supreme Court. The bill was introduced days after gasoline prices peaked in September 2008 and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Energy developers — especially oil and gas companies building pipelines or refineries, and companies seeking leases on federal lands and submerged lands. The bill hands them a way to bypass environmental review, permitting rules, and public objections with a single presidential waiver, shortening the road to construction and revenue.

how_it_helps.text: The bill allows the president or a designee, in their sole discretion, to waive any federal legal requirement applicable to a covered energy project, including rules governing administrative protests of agency decisions.

Covered projects include oil and gas pipelines and refineries and the leasing of federal lands, including submerged lands, for energy exploration, development, production, processing, or transmission.
A determination waiving the law takes effect simply upon publication in the Federal Register, with no approval from Congress or any agency needed.

analysis.who_pays: The public. Ordinary people and communities near projects would lose the normal legal tools to challenge them — environmental protections, permitting requirements, and administrative protest rights could all be waived. The narrow court review (constitutional claims only, within 60 days, appealable only to the Supreme Court) would leave few realistic remedies. Because the bill does not say which laws the president must weigh, any safeguard could be set aside for any project the administration favors.

drawbacks.text: The waiver power covers 'any provision of Federal law' — environmental statutes, public-lands rules, safety requirements — with no standards limiting when it can be used, effectively letting the executive branch set aside laws Congress passed whenever an energy project is involved.

Citizens' ability to contest a project is gutted twice over: administrative protest rights can be waived, and lawsuits are limited to constitutional claims filed within 60 days, reviewable only by the Supreme Court.
Because 'covered energy project' includes routine construction and maintenance of energy facilities, the waiver power would not be limited to large, nationally significant projects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a real goal — faster energy permitting at a time of high fuel prices — but its design went far beyond streamlining. By letting one official suspend any federal law for any energy project, and by closing off nearly all legal challenge, it traded broad, permanent public protections for an open-ended speed advantage for project developers. Even supporters of faster permitting generally pursue narrower fixes for that reason.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with no cosponsors in September 2008, it was referred to three House committees and then to subcommittees, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. John Shadegg introduced the bill on September 11, 2008, during a period of high gasoline prices and intense debate over expanding domestic energy production.
No member joined as a cosponsor.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees on the day it was introduced.
Within days it was sent to the Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee and the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee; the record shows no further action of any kind.
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing system of environmental review, permitting rules, and public protest rights over energy projects stayed intact, and oil, gas, and energy developers did not gain a presidential waiver power. Ordinary people who live near pipelines, refineries, and federal energy leases kept the legal tools the bill would have removed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Environmental safeguards and public legal rights

for.name: Rep. John Shadegg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill granting the president authority to waive any federal law for covered energy projects.

against.name: House subcommittees on Energy and Air Quality and Energy and Mineral Resources
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never reported it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member of either party cosponsored; the only recorded support was the single Republican sponsor.

industries.note: The bill would let the president waive any federal law for pipelines, refineries, and federal-lands drilling leases, cutting permitting time and removing obstacles communities and agencies could raise. The speed and flexibility gained by the industry would come at the cost of the environmental and legal protections ordinary people rely on.

industries.industry: Energy transmission and power facility developers
industries.note: Any facility for developing, producing, processing, or transmitting energy qualifies as covered, so builders of power lines and other energy infrastructure could seek waivers of siting and regulatory requirements. Fewer legal barriers would mean faster projects, with the public bearing the loss of review and protest rights.
